T-series payouts or a systematic withdrawal plan? Drawing cash from a non-registered balanced fund

Compare monthly T-series distributions made mostly of return of capital with selling units through a systematic withdrawal plan, follow the cost base down to zero, and see when the tax deferral helps and when it only moves the bill.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 27 October 2026 · 7 min read
Sources reviewed 27 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Units worth $300,000 with a $180,000 cost base pay 5% of the previous year-end value each year. 2% is the fund’s own taxable income, taxed the same way in both routes and left out of the tax figures; the rest is return of capital in the T-series and a redemption of units in the withdrawal plan. The central idea

Return of capital is not taxed when you receive it, but it lowers your cost base, so the tax arrives later: as a larger gain when you sell, or each year once the cost base reaches zero. With the same tax rate throughout, a T-series and a systematic withdrawal plan from the same fund pay about the same total capital-gains tax; the T-series pays it later. The deferral helps most when the final sale falls in a lower-income year, and the payout rate is not a measure of what the fund earns.

01

Two ways to turn a fund into a monthly cheque

Someone who has built up a balanced fund in a non-registered account, often near or in retirement, eventually wants it to pay a regular amount. Fund companies offer two common routes.

  • A systematic withdrawal plan (SWP) sells enough units each month to pay a chosen amount. Each sale is a disposition, so it can realize a capital gain or loss.
  • A T-series (sold as Series T, T5, T8 or similar) is a series of the same fund that pays a target percentage each year in monthly distributions. RBC Global Asset Management’s description of its Series T, for example, sets the monthly amount as the previous 31 December value per unit times 5% (or 8%) divided by 12, and says return of capital is used to top up the interest, dividends and capital gains the fund earns to reach that rate.

The portfolio and its risk are the same in both routes. What differs is how the cash is labelled for tax, and that changes when tax is paid. This guide follows both routes from the same fund, with the same cash in hand each year.

02

What CRA does with return of capital

CRA’s page on the tax treatment of mutual funds sets out the rules the model uses:

  • A return of capital is not income when received; it reduces the adjusted cost base (ACB) of your units. For a mutual fund trust it is reported in box 42 of the T3 slip. For a mutual fund corporation it is not reported on the T5 slip, so you have to track it yourself.
  • If returns of capital would take the ACB below zero during a year, the negative amount is deemed to be a capital gain in that year and the ACB is reset to zero.
  • When units are sold, the gain is the proceeds minus the ACB, and identical units of the same fund series share one average cost. CRA’s capital gains guide shows half of a capital gain being taxable.

The part of a T-series payout that is the fund’s own interest, dividends or realized gains is taxed in the year received, just as it would be in any other series. The calculator treats that income, 2% of the fund’s value by default, as identical in both routes and leaves its tax out of the comparison. The fund income guide covers how each type is taxed.

03

Following the cost base

The default case starts with units worth CAD 300,000 and an ACB of CAD 180,000, so CAD 120,000 of the value is unrealized gain. Both routes pay 5% of the previous year-end value, CAD 15,000 in year 1. The fund earns a hypothetical 5% a year, so the value and the payout stay level.

The first chart shows the cost base. Of each CAD 15,000, CAD 6,000 is the fund’s income and CAD 9,000 is the rest. In the T-series the full CAD 9,000 is return of capital, so the ACB falls by CAD 9,000 a year and reaches zero in year 20. In the withdrawal plan, each CAD 9,000 sale removes only the cost share of the units sold, so the ACB falls more slowly and is still about CAD 85,969 after 25 years.

The second chart shows the capital-gains tax paid each year at a 30% marginal rate. The withdrawal plan pays some from the start, about CAD 6,591 over the first ten years. The T-series pays none until its ACB is used up; from year 21 CRA deems each year’s CAD 9,000 of return of capital a capital gain, and its annual tax of CAD 1,350 is then higher than the withdrawal plan’s.

04

Deferral, not exemption

The third chart adds the tax due when the remaining units are sold after 25 years. With the same 30% rate throughout, the totals are the same: about CAD 51,750 for each route. That is not a coincidence. Both routes take the same cash out of the same fund and end with the same units, so the total gain is the same; return of capital only changes when it is counted.

The deferral still has value in three situations:

  • A lower rate at the final sale. With the final sale taxed at 20% instead of 30%, the T-series total falls to about CAD 36,750 against CAD 41,048 for the withdrawal plan, because more of its gain waits for the lower rate. Units still held at death are deemed sold at fair market value, so the final rate may be the estate’s final-return rate, not a low one.
  • Income-tested benefits. Return of capital is not income, so lower taxable income in the early years can reduce the OAS recovery tax or keep income below other thresholds. The OAS recovery tax guide shows how those thresholds work.
  • The time value of tax paid later. Money not paid in tax this year can stay invested. That benefit is modest at ordinary returns and is reversed once the ACB reaches zero.

A withdrawal plan from a fund bought recently, near today’s price, also realizes very little gain at first, so the T-series edge is largest for units with a low cost base relative to their value.

05

A payout rate is not a return, and inflation keeps working

The heatmap shows how many years the T-series cost base lasts for payout rates of 4% to 8% and fund returns of 0% to 8%, keeping the default value, cost base and income. Higher payouts use up the cost base faster: at an 8% payout and a 4% return it lasts about 13 years. A cell showing 60 means the cost base lasts at least 60 years, which happens when low returns shrink the fund and the payout with it.

The more important point is what happens to the fund. A distribution that is mostly return of capital is, by definition, partly your own money coming back. If the payout is higher than the fund’s return, the fund shrinks, and because the T-series payout is reset each year on the previous year-end value, the cheque shrinks too. RBC’s description notes that the distribution may be adjusted downward after a year in which the fund falls, which is what happens after a crash. Even when the fund and the payout hold level in dollars, as in the default case, inflation lowers what they buy. The Bank of Canada aims to keep inflation at 2%; at that rate a payout fixed at CAD 15,000 for 25 years buys about 39% less by the end. The balanced fund crash and inflation guide tests withdrawal rates against both risks.

06

Choosing between them

  • Only for non-registered money. In an RRSP, RRIF or TFSA there is no capital gain to defer, so a T-series offers no tax advantage there; every withdrawal from an RRSP or RRIF is taxable and every TFSA withdrawal is tax-free whatever the series.
  • Compare the same fund. T-series and other series of the same fund usually carry the same management fee, but check the Fund Facts; a difference in fees or in advice charges can outweigh a tax deferral.
  • Keep cost-base records. Track the ACB each year from the T3 slips, or yourself for a fund corporation, so the final sale and any deemed gains are reported correctly. The fund cost-base guide shows a ledger.
  • Match the payout to a spending plan, not the other way round. A withdrawal plan lets you choose the amount and pause it; a T-series sets it from the fund’s value. Either can be combined with a cash reserve for the years after a large fall, as the withdrawal sources guide explains.

This guide is a model, not tax advice. Distributions, special year-end capital gains and the mix of return of capital vary by fund and by year; check a specific fund’s documents and confirm a personal case with a tax professional.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 27 October 2026. All four charts use hypothetical editable inputs: fund values, cost bases, returns, payout rates and tax rates are teaching assumptions, not the record or forecast of any fund. The tax rules applied (return of capital reducing the cost base, a negative cost base deemed a capital gain, one-half inclusion) are from CRA pages reviewed 27 October 2026. The payout mechanics follow one fund company’s published description of its Series T, used as an example. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. Canada Revenue Agency · Tax treatment of mutual funds ↗

    Page dated 5 February 2026; reviewed 27 October 2026. A return of capital reduces the adjusted cost base; T3 box 42 amounts adjust the ACB of mutual fund trust units; if the ACB is reduced below zero, the negative amount is deemed a capital gain in the year and the new ACB is deemed to be zero; returns of capital on mutual fund corporation shares are not reported on the T5 slip; identical units use an average cost.

  2. Canada Revenue Agency · Calculating and reporting your capital gains and losses ↗

    Page dated 5 February 2026; reviewed 27 October 2026 for the statement that 50% of a capital gain is taxable, used as the one-half inclusion rate.

  3. RBC Global Asset Management · How does Series T provide tax-efficient cash flow? ↗

    Used as one fund company’s example of how a T-series works: monthly distribution equal to the previous 31 December net asset value per unit times 5% (Series T5) or 8% (Series T8) divided by 12; return of capital used to top up the fund’s income to the payout rate; distribution adjusted downward after a year the fund falls; a systematic withdrawal plan may trigger capital gains on each sale. Text read from a copy captured 10 August 2026; the page returned HTTP 200 on 27 October 2026. Not a recommendation of any fund.

  4. Bank of Canada · Inflation ↗

    Reviewed 27 October 2026 for the statement that the Bank aims to keep inflation at the 2% midpoint of a 1% to 3% target range, used for the purchasing-power example.
